unitDescription.value: In this unit, students will design and develop a digital game using GDevelop. They will begin by exploring how game engines work, including frames, inputs, events, collisions, movement, graphics, and the game loop. Students will practise decomposing simple games into smaller systems and create a basic prototype before beginning their major project. For the assignment, students will work in groups to research existing games, analyse user experience, and design an original or modified game concept that considers flow, challenge, feedback, clarity, and player engagement. Using agile project management methods, students will create a Kanban board, break their project into manageable tasks, hold regular team meetings, and iteratively develop their game through prototyping, testing, feedback, and refinement. By the end of the unit, students will produce a playable game and evaluate how effectively their design decisions, development process, and final product meet the intended user experience.

cohortAndClassConsiderations.value: The Years 9–10 cohort consists of a diverse group of boys with a wide range of digital competencies, from students with strong technical skills and personal interest in IT, to those who require further support to confidently engage with digital systems. Many students come from regional or rural backgrounds, where access to structured digital learning opportunities may have been limited. The program is designed to build on prior knowledge while introducing more advanced and applied skills relevant to future study and employment. The curriculum supports the school’s priority to equip students with transferable digital skills, critical thinking abilities, and an understanding of ethical technology use in a rapidly changing world.

description.value:
In this assignment, students will work in groups to design and develop a playable digital game using GDevelop. Students will begin by researching existing games and analysing how user experience features such as controls, feedback, challenge, flow, visuals, instructions, and level design affect player engagement. They will then create their own game concept, decompose it into smaller systems, and plan the development process using agile project management methods.

Each group will create and maintain a Kanban board in Trello to organise tasks, manage responsibilities, track progress, and respond to problems during development. Students will build their game through prototyping, testing, feedback, and refinement. They will collect player feedback, make improvements based on that feedback, and keep evidence of their design and development process.

The final submission will include a playable GDevelop game, evidence of planning and project management, research into existing games, design documentation, testing and feedback evidence, and an evaluation of how effectively the final game meets the intended user experience.

achievementStandard.value: By the end of Year 10 students develop and modify innovative digital solutions, decompose real-world problems, and critically evaluate alternative solutions against stakeholder elicited user stories. Students acquire, interpret and model complex data with databases and represent documents as content, structure and presentation. They design and validate algorithms and implement them, including in an object-oriented programming language. Students explain how digital systems manage, control and secure access to data; and model cyber security threats and explore a vulnerability. They use advanced features of digital tools to create interactive content, and to plan, collaborate on, and manage agile projects. Students apply privacy principles to manage digital footprints.

lessons.title: Demystifying Game Engines & The Game Loop
lessons.learningGoal: Explain the architectural phases of the game loop and the role of event-driven programming within a game engine.

orientate.smartStart: On the board, write down three everyday systems that continuously wait for user input, process it, and update their state (e.g., an ATM, a microwave, or a smartphone touchscreen). Briefly explain how they resemble a game.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain the three phases of the game loop and distinguish event-driven programming from procedural coding

activities.title: Decoding Game Engine Architecture Vocabulary
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher presents the core architecture of a game engine, using the analogy of a continuous 'pulse' or 'heartbeat'. Model the distinction between a passive software application (like a calculator that executes code only upon input) and a game engine (which cycles input-process-render thousands of times per minute). Provide an example: 'When you press the jump key, the engine doesn't wait; it registers the input during the next tick, updates the Y-coordinate of the character, and re-renders the frame immediately.'
activities.studentsDo: Students complete the matching matrix in their workbook to establish precise definitions for technical terminology. They must link the architectural terms (Game Loop, Event-Driven, Tick Rate, Rendering) to the provided functional descriptions.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the Game Engine Architecture Matrix. In the 'Match' column, write the letter (A-D) corresponding to the correct definition from the bank below. Ensure you understand the distinction between the 'Game Loop' and 'Tick Rate' before submitting.
activities.questioning:
question: What would happen to a multiplayer shooter game if its tick rate dropped from 60Hz to 10Hz?
expected: The game state would update significantly slower, causing perceived 'lag', delayed input registration, and visual stuttering, as physics and positions are calculated only 10 times per second rather than 60.
question: Why is a modern digital game considered 'event-driven' rather than purely procedural?
expected: Because the game engine remains in a continuous state of listening for specific conditions (events) like keystrokes, mouse clicks, or collisions, and triggers corresponding logic in response, rather than executing lines of code in a single linear sequence from top to bottom.
activities.scaffolding:
Game Loop: A continuous loop that runs during gameplay to handle input, update game state, and render graphics. 
Event-Driven: A programming paradigm where the flow of the program is determined by events such as user actions or sensor outputs. 
Tick Rate: The frequency (measured in Hertz) at which a game engine executes its game loop calculations per second. 
Rendering: The process of generating a 2D or 3D image on screen from a game's model data.
activities.eLearning: Project the GDevelop interface on the main screen to illustrate the loop visually while students complete the definitions.
activities.transition: Now that we have established the architectural vocabulary, we will examine how the game loop sequences these tasks every fraction of a second to create real-time interactivity.

workbookSpec.title: Game Engine Architecture Matrix
bank: A. The continuous process of drawing updated game graphics, sprites, and backgrounds to the screen.
B. The master software loop that polls for user input, updates positions, physics, and displays frames.
C. System where events (collisions, inputs) trigger specific response blocks rather than linear step-by-step execution.
D. The number of times per second the game engine updates its logic and processes frames (e.g., 60 Hz).

activities.workbookMaterials: Vocabulary matching matrix on Game Engine Architecture.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: Game Loop: B. Event-Driven Programming: C. Tick Rate: D. Rendering: A.

activities.title: Anatomy of the Game Loop
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher displays the game loop cycle and explains that the loop repeats constantly, often 60 times per second. Modelled example: 'If I press the right arrow key, the Input phase captures that intent; the Update phase processes the movement math; the Render phase draws the sprite at the new position. If one phase takes too long, the 'frame' cannot complete on time, causing visual stuttering.'
activities.studentsDo: Students follow along with the lecture by completing the Cloze paragraph in their printed workbook, ensuring they understand the sequential logic of the Input-Update-Render cycle.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the 'Anatomy of the Game Loop' Cloze paragraph using the terms provided in the word bank to accurately describe the frame life cycle.
activities.questioning:
question: If the Update step takes too long to compute physics, what happens to the subsequent Render step?
expected: The Render step will be delayed, leading to a dropped frame or low frame rate, which the player experiences as visual stuttering or 'lag'.
question: Why is the loop typically run 60 times per second rather than just once?
expected: To ensure fluid, responsive, and real-time interaction; anything significantly slower appears as a series of static images rather than smooth animation.
activities.scaffolding: Input Phase: Captures user actions (keyboard, mouse, touch). Update Phase: Processes internal logic (physics, collisions, state changes). Render Phase: Draws the visual output to the screen. Frame: One complete cycle of this loop.
activities.eLearning: Project the 'Anatomy of the Game Loop' diagram on the main screen. Students must keep laptops closed until the completion of this note-taking activity.
activities.transition: Now that we have defined the engine's internal logic, we will open GDevelop to identify these specific phases in the event sheet interface.

Finally, the {{5}} phase updates the screen with the new positions of sprites. For smooth motion, this cycle should ideally occur {{6}} times per second.

activities.title: Mapping Interactive Game Actions
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher displays a visual diagram of the Game Loop (Input-Update-Render) on the board. The teacher models the 'Jump' scenario decomposition: Input (Keyboard 'Space' pressed), Update (Velocity Y set to -500; gravity constant applied), and Render (Sprite swapped to 'jumping_frame_01'). The teacher monitors student analysis of the three scenarios, providing corrective feedback on the distinction between logic (Update) and visual output (Render).
activities.studentsDo: Students complete the decomposition table in their workbooks for three specific game interactions. They must isolate the precise input trigger, the resulting logic change in the engine, and the final frame composition.
activities.visibleInstructions: Analyze the three provided scenarios. For each, complete the decomposition table by identifying the distinct Input, Update, and Render stages. Ensure your descriptions use technical terminology: Input (Event trigger), Update (Mathematical/Logic change), and Render (Visual output).
activities.questioning:
question: If a character stops moving, is the Render stage still running?
expected: Yes. The loop must continue to render the scene at 60 FPS (or the monitor refresh rate) even if the object's positional data remains static, ensuring the game does not freeze.
question: Why must the Update phase occur before the Render phase?
expected: The engine must calculate the new game state (e.g., enemy position) before it can draw the pixels representing that new state; otherwise, the player would see delayed or inaccurate movement.
activities.scaffolding: Reference Table: Input (User action or system trigger) -> Update (Variables, velocity, health, physics calculations) -> Render (Visual refresh of screen/frame). Example: A projectile firing involves an Input (Click), an Update (Calculate trajectory/collision bounds), and a Render (Draw sprite at new X/Y).
activities.eLearning: Laptops remain closed. Students use hard-copy workbooks to ensure focus on architectural concepts rather than GDevelop interface navigation.
activities.transition: Transitioning from these conceptual flows to GDevelop's event sheet, where we will soon write code to handle these precise Input-Update-Render cycles.

workbookSpec.prompt: Decompose the following three game scenarios into their core architectural phases.

sections.label: Scenario 2: Enemy patrol touches a boundary

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Scenario 1 (Jump): Input: Spacebar event detected. Update: Set velocity Y to negative value; apply gravity constant. Render: Update sprite animation to 'jump_state'. Scenario 2 (Patrol): Input: Collision detected (System trigger). Update: Multiply X velocity by -1. Render: Flip sprite horizontally. Scenario 3 (Health): Input: Collision/damage event. Update: Health variable = Health - 10; check if Health <= 0. Render: Remove player sprite; initiate 'Game Over' screen overlay.

culminate.summarise: We reviewed the internal architecture of game engines. We tracked how input translates to system changes and visual renderings dozens of times every second.

lessons.title: Creating Objects, Sprites & Layers
lessons.learningGoal: Create, modify, and coordinate spatial positions of 2D game sprites across multiple layers inside GDevelop.

orientate.smartStart: On your blank worksheet, write down the definition of a 'Sprite' in your own words, and list two classic games that rely entirely on 2D sprite graphics.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can create a Sprite object, edit its visual properties, and position it on different canvas layers

activities.title: Creating and Importing Sprite Objects
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher demonstrates the workflow for object creation in GDevelop. The teacher selects 'Add a new object', chooses 'Sprite', and renames it to 'PlayerSprite'. Using the built-in Piskel editor, the teacher draws a simple geometric shape, saves it, and adds it to the project. The teacher then drags this object onto the canvas, highlighting how the Properties Panel updates to show X and Y coordinates. The teacher models the 'blueprint vs. instance' concept by editing the parent object and observing that all instances on the canvas update simultaneously. Example script: 'Note that the object in the panel is the master record. When I change the colour here, every instance on the board reflects the change because they are linked to this source.'
activities.studentsDo: Students observe the teacher’s screen to identify the hierarchy between the object definition and the scene instances. Students document the definitions provided in the scaffolding section within their workbooks to internalise the relationship between project assets and scene placement.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher demonstration. Watch how the Properties Panel dynamically changes when a sprite is selected. Complete the definitions of 'Object' and 'Instance' in your workbook to solidify your understanding of game asset architecture.
activities.questioning:
question: What happens to all instances on the screen if we edit the primary sprite image in the Object panel?
expected: All instances update instantly because they refer back to the same parent object definition.
question: If an object's position is X: 0, Y: 0, where will it appear on the screen?
expected: At the top-left corner of the game window coordinates (origin point).
activities.scaffolding:
Object: The master template/blueprint created in the project objects panel. It holds the core logic, animations, and behaviours.
Instance: A unique, placed copy of that object in the active game scene, possessing its own independent coordinate metadata (X/Y position) and Z-order/layer.
activities.eLearning: Students must keep laptops closed during the teacher demonstration of the Piskel editor to ensure full attention to the interface navigation.
activities.transition: Transitioning from observation to application: Please open your GDevelop projects. We will now create your own PlayerSprite and a ground block using the techniques just demonstrated.

workbookSpec.title: Game Object Architecture
workbookSpec.prompt: Distinguish between the parent object definition and individual scene instances.

sections.label: Justification: Why do we edit the 'Object' rather than the individual 'Instance' when changing a character's colour?

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Object: The master blueprint created in the objects panel. It is the single source of truth for the asset's properties. Instance: A unique, placed copy of that object in the active game scene, containing its own coordinate metadata. Justification: Editing the parent Object ensures that every instance is updated simultaneously (DRY principle), maintaining consistency across the game and preventing the need to manually update every copy placed in a level.

activities.title: Adding Objects & Coordinating Spatial Properties
activities.teacherDoes: Teacher demonstrates the instantiation of objects and spatial manipulation using the Properties Panel. Script: 'Observe the Properties panel on the right. When I select my green Player sprite, notice the X and Y coordinates. If I change Y from 300 to 400, watch the sprite descend. This coordinate system is standard across most 2D engines: (0,0) is top-left, meaning increasing Y values move objects down. When placing platforms, ensure you are snapping them to the grid to maintain visual consistency.' Model example: 'Watch as I duplicate the Platform object using Ctrl+D to maintain identical dimensions for the floor.'
activities.studentsDo: Students follow the demonstration to create a 'Player' object using the Piskel editor and a 'Platform' object. They place the player at (100, 300) and construct a floor using multiple Platform instances aligned at Y: 550. Students must use the Properties Panel for precise coordinate placement rather than relying solely on drag-and-drop.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Open the GDevelop project and create a new Sprite object named 'Player'. 2. Paint a simple green square in the Piskel editor and save. 3. Drag the Player into the Level1 scene. 4. In the Properties panel, set Position: X = 100, Y = 300. 5. Create a second Sprite named 'Platform', paint it brown, and place multiple instances to create a floor at Y = 550. 6. Verify your progress using the checklist.
activities.questioning:
question: What happens to the spatial position of our Player sprite if we increase the Y coordinate value in the Properties panel?
expected: The sprite moves downwards on the screen because the GDevelop coordinate system originates at the top-left (0,0) and increases as you move down.
question: Why is it preferable to use the Properties panel to set coordinates rather than dragging objects with the mouse?
expected: Manual entry ensures pixel-perfect alignment and prevents inconsistent spacing between floor segments, which is critical for smooth character movement.
activities.scaffolding:
Coordinate System Summary: 
X-Axis: Horizontal movement (left to right, 0 to screen width). 
Y-Axis: Vertical movement (top to bottom, 0 to screen height). 
Properties Panel: The primary interface for controlling Object Name, X/Y Position, Size, and Opacity. 
Snapping: Use the grid (toggle with Ctrl+G) to ensure platforms align perfectly on the same Y-axis plane.
activities.eLearning: Monitor student workstations to ensure they are using the Properties panel input fields rather than mouse-positioning. Check that Object names follow naming conventions (e.g., 'Player', 'Platform') for future reference in the Event Sheet.

activities.title: Layering and Z-Order Control
activities.teacherDoes: The teacher demonstrates how layering and Z-ordering function as independent axes in GDevelop: 'Layers act as global rendering buckets, while Z-Order acts as local sorting within those buckets.' Model: Place a background image on a 'Background' layer (Z=0) and a player sprite on the 'Base' layer (Z=100). Show how changing the layer of an object instantly re-sorts the entire scene composition, whereas changing Z-order only impacts overlaps within the same layer.
activities.studentsDo: Students configure their project layers, assign assets to the 'Background', 'Environment', and 'HUD' layers, and populate the configuration table to verify their organizational structure.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Open the Layers panel in GDevelop. 2. Create new layers: 'Background', 'Environment', and 'UI'. 3. Assign your game objects to the correct layer. 4. Complete the Layer Configuration audit table to confirm the visual hierarchy of your scene.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the primary difference between a layer and Z-order when organising game assets?
expected: Layers are independent rendering planes drawn in a specific sequence (top to bottom), whereas Z-order determines sorting priority only for objects sharing the exact same layer.
question: If your UI buttons are appearing behind the player sprite, which property should you adjust?
expected: The Layer property. The UI should be on a separate 'UI' or 'Top' layer that is positioned above the 'Base' layer in the layer list.

activities.title: Core Vocabulary of Event-Driven Logic
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the event-driven architecture used by modern game engines like GDevelop. Model the concept: 'Conditions' (If) act as gates, and 'Actions' (Then) act as the output. Provide the analogy: If [Doorbell rings], Then [Play sound]. Explain that computational thinking requires decomposing complex player mechanics into these discrete 'If-Then' pairs to prevent logic errors.
activities.studentsDo: Review the provided scaffolding definitions. Complete the matching table in the workbook by associating each technical term with its correct definition from the bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the definitions provided in Section 1, complete the table by matching the correct programming Term to its definition found in the word bank.
activities.questioning:
Why is a game engine considered 'event-driven' rather than just running code top-to-bottom once? Expected: Because it must constantly listen for user inputs and game changes in a continuous loop to check if conditions are met.
What is the difference between a condition and an action in GDevelop? Expected: A condition is a test or boolean check that must evaluate to True, whereas an action is the subsequent command or behavior executed when that test is satisfied.
activities.scaffolding:
Event: A block of logic containing conditions and actions that dictate game behavior.
Condition: A test or trigger (such as key press or collision) that must evaluate to True for the event to execute.
Action: The resulting change in the game state (such as moving an object or playing a sound) when conditions are met.
Decomposition: Breaking a complex system or mechanic down into smaller, manageable, logical steps.

expected: GDevelop will run the actions constantly on every single frame of the game loop, which usually causes glitches or unintended behaviour.

expected: They are indented beneath the parent event, indicating that they only execute if the parent condition is true.

2. Conditions: The 'If' statement (what must be true).
3. Actions: The 'Then' statement (what occurs).
4. Frame: A single update cycle (usually 60 per second).
5. Indented: Visual hierarchy showing dependency.

activities.title: I Do: Spatial Coordinate Manipulation in 2D Engines
activities.teacherDoes: Display the coordinate plane diagram on the projector. Delivery script: 'In GDevelop, the screen origin (0,0) is pinned to the top-left corner. Unlike the standard Cartesian plane taught in Mathematics, the Y-axis in game engines is inverted: values increase as you move down the screen. To make a sprite move, we must manipulate these values. For example, to move right, we apply an action: Change the X position of Player, set to Player.X() + 5. Observe this diagram; let us annotate the coordinate shifts together.'

activities.questioning:
How does GDevelop's Y-axis orientation differ from the standard Cartesian plane used in Mathematics? Expected: In GDevelop, Y increases as you move down the screen, whereas in Mathematics, Y increases as you move up.
If we want a sprite to move left across the screen, what coordinate change must we apply? Expected: We must subtract from the object's X coordinate (X - speed).
activities.scaffolding:
Movement Logic Summary:
- Up: Y-axis decreases (-)
- Down: Y-axis increases (+)
- Left: X-axis decreases (-)
- Right: X-axis increases (+)

activities.title: I Do: Explaining Hitboxes vs. Sprite Visuals
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the distinction between a 'hitbox' (collision mask) and the visual sprite. Project a GDevelop window. Model the process: 1. Open 'Edit Collision Masks'. 2. Compare a default rectangular mask vs. a complex polygon mask. Script: 'The engine treats hitboxes as simplified mathematical shapes because checking intersection for 4,000 pixels is slower than checking for 4 corners.' Show an example where a character is 'stuck' due to an oversized hitbox. Model how to tighten the padding.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the projection of the collision mask editor. Engage in the annotation activity in Section 1 to identify the relationship between performance and hitbox complexity.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. View the sprite image provided in your workbook. 2. Use the numbered callouts to annotate the diagram as I demonstrate on the projector. 3. Complete the definition bank to finalise your understanding of collision terminology.
activities.questioning:
question: Why don't we draw an extremely detailed collision shape that traces every pixel of our character?
expected: It is computationally heavy for the game engine to calculate complex shapes in real-time. Simplified shapes increase engine efficiency (performance).
question: What is a common consequence of having a hitbox that is much larger than the visual sprite?
expected: The player feels like they are getting hit by obstacles or enemies when they haven't visually touched them yet, leading to 'unfair' gameplay mechanics.
activities.scaffolding: TERMINOLOGY: Hitbox (Collision Mask) - An invisible, simplified polygon used by the game engine to detect overlaps. | PERFORMANCE COST - The computational resource required to calculate physics logic. | PAD/PADDING - The gap between the sprite's visual edge and the actual hitbox boundary.

activities.title: We Do: Setting up Collision Triggers
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the logic flow required for object interaction. Model the process: 'Condition: If Player collides with Item; Action: Delete Item. Why do we include the delete action? Because the game engine refreshes 60 times per second; without deletion, the collision event continues to trigger indefinitely.' Guide students through the GDevelop 'New Event' interface, emphasising the distinction between condition checks and resultant actions.

question: Why must we delete the 'Gem' sprite instantly when the collision is triggered?
expected: If the sprite is not deleted, the collision condition remains true on every frame of the game, causing events such as sound triggers or score increments to execute infinitely.
question: What action would we use instead of deletion if we wanted the player to bounce off an obstacle?
expected: We would use physical forces or separation logic, such as reversing the player's velocity on that axis or using the 'Separate objects' action.
activities.scaffolding:
Collision Logic Structure: 
1. Condition: A Boolean state check (Are these two hitboxes overlapping?)
2. Action: The game engine task performed if the condition evaluates to True.
3. Procedural steps: Add Condition -> Common Conditions -> Collisions -> Collision. Select objects. Add Action -> Delete Object.

activities.title: You Do: Preventing Wall Phase-Throughs
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate the room to monitor GDevelop workspace configurations. Model the logic: 'Condition: Player collides with Wall; Action: Separate Player from Wall'. Check that students identify the 'Player' as the object being acted upon. Use the following prompt to check for understanding: 'If your player is still passing through the wall, check if your Wall sprite has the Physics behavior or the Platformer Obstacle behavior enabled, as the collision mask relies on these properties.'
activities.studentsDo: Add a Wall sprite to the GDevelop scene and apply the 'Platformer Obstacle' behavior. Create the event that triggers the 'Separate objects' action to ensure the Player cannot move through solid barriers. Complete the reflection in the workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Configure the Wall behavior as a 'Platformer Obstacle'. 2. Create an event: Collision between Player and Wall. 3. Add the action 'Separate objects' (Player from Wall). 4. Preview the game and document your observations.
activities.questioning:
question: What occurs if the order of separation is reversed (e.g., Separate Wall from Player)?
expected: The Wall object would be displaced or pushed if it were not static, or the collision detection would fail to lock the player's position effectively because the logic is checking the wrong object's boundary.
question: How does this separation logic improve player experience?
expected: It creates physical boundaries that enforce the intended game map, preventing 'clipping' bugs where players pass through solid terrain, which maintains immersion and map integrity.
activities.scaffolding: Logic Checklist: 1. Ensure the Wall sprite has the 'Platformer Obstacle' behavior added in the properties panel. 2. Event Structure: 'If Player is in collision with Wall' -> 'Separate Player from Wall'. 3. If the character jitters, ensure the collision mask is set to 'Automatic' in the sprite editor.

workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the outcome of your collision logic implementation.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Delete removes the object (e.g., coins/power-ups), whereas Separate prevents movement overlap (e.g., walls/floors). 2. The obstacle behavior defines the hitbox and physical properties that GDevelop uses to calculate the separation distance. 3. A locked door or a heavy crate that the player can push but not walk through.

sections.label: 1. Describe the difference in game behavior between a 'Delete' action on collision versus a 'Separate' action on collision.
2. Explain why assigning the 'Platformer Obstacle' behavior to your wall is a prerequisite for the 'Separate' action to function correctly.
3. Identify one other game object in a platformer that would require a 'Separate' action instead of a 'Delete' action.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Delete action removes the target object permanently from the scene, which is used for consumables like coins or items collected. The Separate action does not remove the object but calculates the distance needed to push the player back outside the object's hitbox, preventing overlapping and phase-through glitches. 2. The 'Platformer Obstacle' behavior defines the collision boundaries (hitbox) and physical solidity. Without this behavior, the engine may not recognise the wall as a physical entity to separate from. 3. Example: A crate or a non-player character (NPC) that acts as a physical barrier but remains present in the scene.

question: What is the primary technical risk of failing to define an MVP early in development?
expected: Over-engineering features that do not enhance the core 'game feel', resulting in wasted development time and potential scope creep.
activities.scaffolding:
Agile Vocabulary Key Definitions:
1. Sprint: A set period during which specific work must be completed and made ready for review.
2. Kanban: A framework used to implement Agile by visualizing work, limiting work-in-progress, and maximizing efficiency.
3. MVP (Minimum Viable Product): The version of a new product which allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning with the least effort.
4. Iteration: The repetition of a process in order to generate a sequence of outcomes; each iteration aims to improve the product based on previous feedback.
activities.eLearning: Monitor individual student progress during the activity. Ensure students are correctly identifying 'Iteration' vs 'Sprint' as these are frequently confused.
activities.transition: Now that we have established the Agile lexicon, we will apply these concepts to our practical Kanban board setup.

activities.title: MVP Concept Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the concept of a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) using a simple analogy: if a car is the final goal, the MVP is not a wheel, but a skateboard. Use the board to sort features like 'Jump Mechanics' vs 'Background Music'. Model the classification: 'Jump mechanics are non-negotiable for a platformer; therefore, they are an MVP feature. Background music adds polish, but the game functions without it; therefore, it is secondary.'
activities.studentsDo: Analyze a list of five core and secondary game features. Complete the cloze-style guided notes to justify why specific mechanics are categorized as MVP essentials versus secondary polish, ensuring their project roadmap prioritizes functional integrity.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the cloze sentences below by selecting the appropriate term from the word bank to justify feature prioritization in game development.
activities.questioning:
question: If you have limited time to complete your build, which group of features must be finished first?
expected: The MVP features must be finished first because they represent the core mechanics required for the game to function at a playable level.
question: Why is 'High-definition 3D textures' usually excluded from an MVP?
expected: It is considered decorative polish; the game can still be tested and validated for its core mechanics (like physics or collision) without high-fidelity graphics.
activities.scaffolding: MVP = Minimum Viable Product. Essential Features: The minimum set of core mechanics required for the product to function. Without these, the game is unplayable or broken. Secondary Features: Enhancements, aesthetic polish, and additional content that improve the user experience but are not required for the game to be functional.

activities.title: I-Do: The White-Box Prototype
activities.teacherDoes: Launch GDevelop and create a new scene. Add a tiled sprite for the floor and a simple square for the player character. Model the 'Platformer Object' behaviour, highlighting how simple primitives isolate game feel from artistic asset creation. Demonstrate how white-boxing isolates physics logic: explain that 'if the player is on the floor AND Space is pressed, trigger jump'. Clearly define these as Event 1 (Physics/Conditions) and Event 2 (Trigger/Action).
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration of primitive asset manipulation. Document the identified logic structures in the workbook to build a technical reference for their own prototyping.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher-led prototype construction. Record the key logical events required to establish basic character physics in GDevelop.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is 'white-boxing' (using simple geometry) essential during the early prototyping phase?
expected: It allows developers to isolate and refine game mechanics and physics feel without the distraction of artistic assets, making it easier to diagnose logical errors.
question: What is the primary risk of using high-fidelity assets before establishing core movement mechanics?
expected: High-fidelity assets create 'sunk cost' bias and increase technical complexity, making it harder to debug physics interactions or performance bottlenecks.
activities.scaffolding: Core Mechanics Scaffolding: 1. Platformer Character Behaviour: Adds velocity, gravity, and collision detection automatically. 2. Jump Event Logic: Condition (Key Space Pressed) + Action (Simulate Jump Key). 3. Grounded State: Condition (Player is on floor).

activities.transition: Transition: Now we try this together.

sections.label: Rationale: Why ignore graphics during this stage?

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Physical Constraint: Platformer Character behavior applied to object (defines gravity/velocity). 2. Movement Trigger: 'Key Space Pressed' linked to 'Simulate Jump' action. activities.title: We-Do: Prototyping Constraints
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate how to locate the Player object properties in GDevelop. Model the adjustment of the 'Max Speed' variable from 200 to 800 to demonstrate physics breakdown. Introduce the concept of a 'Technical Constraint Check' as part of agile testing. Example: 'When I increase the speed, the character moves faster than the collision detection can calculate, causing the character to pass through the wall boundary.'
activities.studentsDo: Navigate to the Player object properties panel. Conduct iterative tests by adjusting speed and jump height. Evaluate each mechanic against the checklist criteria in your workbook, ensuring that the collision engine maintains integrity without clipping.
activities.visibleInstructions: Systematically verify your character's physics. Use the provided checklist in your workbook to document successful mechanic implementation and identify any performance bottlenecks that require further debugging.
activities.questioning:
question: What is the specific technical constraint that causes the character to phase through walls at high speeds?
expected: The collision detection algorithm cannot keep up with the frame-to-frame movement speed (velocity), resulting in missed collision checks.
question: Why is it important to define an 'MVP' (Minimum Viable Product) mechanic before adding secondary features?
expected: It allows developers to isolate and fix physics-based bugs before complex assets or code layers are added, which makes debugging significantly harder.
activities.scaffolding:
Checklist Protocol for Prototype Testing:
1. Variable Identification: Locating properties (Speed/Gravity/JumpForce).
2. Collision Integrity: Testing boundaries (Wall/Floor/Ceiling).
3. Iteration: Adjusting one variable at a time.
4. Documentation: Recording the 'breaking point' where the mechanic fails.
activities.eLearning: Monitor students in GDevelop via the project dashboard. Ensure they are using the 'Preview' function correctly to test physics changes.
activities.transition: Now that you have verified your core movement mechanics, you will next formalize your findings in the project log.

workbookSpec.title: Movement Prototype Verification
workbookSpec.prompt: Verify the following mechanics and document technical constraints.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All boxes must be ticked for a successful build; 'no' answers indicate a need for further collision debugging.
items: Player moves horizontally at consistent speed
Gravity correctly pulls player to platform surface
Jump velocity prevents ceiling clipping
No collision 'phasing' occurs at maximum speed settings
Mechanic reset function (re-spawn) works correctly

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Successful implementation is evidenced by the player interacting with collisions predictably. Failure criteria (Technical constraints): 1. Clipping detected at speeds > 600px/s (adjust collision mask), 2. Jump force inconsistent due to gravity scaling (check gravity multiplier), 3. Variable variables inconsistent (ensure 'Global' vs 'Object' variable scope is correct).

activities.title: You-Do: Identify Bottlenecks
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate a common 'double-jump' logic error where the gravity variable conflicts with state checking. Model the thinking process: 'My logic says jump if Y velocity is 0, but the player is rarely exactly 0 due to engine friction. My wireframe needs a state variable to track if the jump button was pressed while in air.'
activities.studentsDo: Students will rapidly prototype a 'double jump' or 'wall jump' mechanic in GDevelop. They must document the specific wireframe logic that failed, explaining the technical bottleneck encountered during the iterative build.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Prototype your mechanic in GDevelop. 2. Use the wireframe template to map out the logic flow (Input -> Condition -> Result). 3. Identify and document one specific technical constraint or bottleneck you encountered.
activities.questioning:
question: What state management is required to distinguish a first jump from a second jump?
expected: A boolean variable or counter that tracks whether the player has already used their air-jump allowance.
question: How does engine friction or gravity acceleration complicate simple 'if-then' logic in platformers?
expected: Variable frame rates and continuous acceleration mean physics calculations rarely return exact integer values, requiring thresholds or epsilon comparisons.
activities.scaffolding: Logic Flow Pattern: [Trigger (Input)] -> [Check (State Variable)] -> [Action (Physics Impulse)]. Bottleneck Examples: 1. Infinite air jumps (logic doesn't reset on landing). 2. Input latency (button press ignored during animation transition). 3. Collision detection failure (wall jump triggers while standing on ground).
activities.eLearning: GDevelop Prototyping Environment; Trello board for logging technical debt.
activities.transition: Transition: Save your GDevelop project. We will shift focus to debugging these specific technical hurdles in the next session.

activities.title: Bug-Hunting Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the GDevelop Debugger interface, specifically highlighting the 'Variable Inspector' panel. I will execute a 'broken' game event—a health variable that fails to clamp at zero, causing negative health—and show how the Debugger identifies the specific event block responsible. Model the correct categorization of this issue as 'High' severity, as it impacts core gameplay mechanics, compared to a 'Low' severity visual clipping error.
activities.studentsDo: Identify and document technical bugs within the current prototype using the Debugger tool. Categorize each bug based on the defined severity levels and update your Kanban board status for these tasks.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the provided audit table to document three distinct bugs discovered during your prototyping session. Assign a severity level to each and verify the technical cause using the GDevelop Debugger.
activities.questioning:
question: If the Debugger shows a variable value changing unexpectedly, what does this tell us about our logic events?
expected: It indicates that the specific condition triggering the change has been met erroneously or lacks appropriate constraints, suggesting a logic error in event sequencing.
question: Why is it critical to distinguish between a 'High' and 'Low' severity bug when managing your project?
expected: Distinguishing severity allows for prioritized resource allocation; high-severity bugs block core gameplay and require immediate resolution, while low-severity issues can be addressed during the final polish phase.
activities.scaffolding: Severity Levels: High (Game-breaking, crashes, core logic failure, prevents progression). Low (Visual-only glitches, incorrect text display, minor animation desync). Debugging Steps: 1. Reproduce error. 2. Open Debugger. 3. Monitor specific object variables. 4. Isolate faulty event block.
activities.eLearning: Open GDevelop. Use CTRL+SHIFT+P (or Debug menu) to launch the Debugger alongside the preview window.
activities.transition: After completing this audit, update your Trello Kanban board: move 'Resolved' items to Done and add new 'Bug Fix' cards to your To-Do list.

question: Why do we prioritize 'High' severity bugs before adding new game features?
expected: Critical bugs block the core gameplay loop; features are unstable until foundational mechanics function correctly.
question: What is the danger of attempting to fix multiple low-priority bugs simultaneously?
expected: Loss of focus on the minimum viable product (MVP) and risk of introducing new regressions without clear testing.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Player Experience: Flow & Challenge
lessons.learningGoal: Evaluate game mechanics using the concepts of 'Flow' and 'Challenge Curve' to explain player engagement.

orientate.smartStart: Students rank three game scenarios (Easy, Balanced, Impossible) in terms of player boredom versus frustration.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can evaluate how game difficulty creates 'Flow' in player experiences

activities.title: Defining Core UX Concepts
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the 'Flow Channel' theory using a line graph projection on the whiteboard. Differentiate between 'Flow' (optimal engagement), 'Boredom' (low challenge), and 'Anxiety' (excessive challenge). Provide a brief demonstration: 'In a game like Super Mario, the first level is a tutorial—low challenge, low anxiety—placing the player in Flow. If the difficulty spikes immediately to a late-game boss level, the player hits the Frustration Threshold and disengages.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the vocabulary definition table by matching the correct UX terminology to its academic definition.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the provided word bank to complete the definitions table. Ensure your definitions reflect the relationship between player skill and game difficulty.
activities.questioning: How does the 'Frustration Threshold' differ from 'Challenge'? Expected: Challenge is a mechanic meant to engage; the Frustration Threshold is a psychological limit where challenge exceeds the player's capacity, causing cessation of play. Why is a static difficulty level detrimental to long-term engagement? Expected: It fails to accommodate the player's increasing mastery, leading to boredom once the challenge no longer tests their skill.
activities.scaffolding: Flow State: An optimal experience where perceived challenges align with perceived skills. Challenge Curve: The arc of difficulty across a gameplay session. Frustration Threshold: The specific point at which a player perceives difficulty as unfair or insurmountable.
activities.eLearning: Project the 'Flow Channel' diagram and a brief video on 'balancing game difficulty' to assist with conceptual understanding.
activities.transition: Move into the comparative analysis workshop where these concepts will be applied to current mobile game case studies.

workbookSpec.title: UX Terminology Audit
bank: The point at which game difficulty exceeds a player's ability and motivation, resulting in disengagement.
A mental state of full immersion where a player's skill set perfectly matches the game's challenge.
The visual or logical progression of difficulty levels designed to keep players in a state of optimal engagement.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Flow: A mental state of full immersion where a player's skill set perfectly matches the game's challenge. Challenge Curve: The visual or logical progression of difficulty levels designed to keep players in a state of optimal engagement. Frustration Threshold: The point at which game difficulty exceeds a player's ability and motivation, resulting in disengagement.

activities.title: Mapping Difficulty Progression
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that game 'Flow' is maintained by balancing difficulty curves against player skill. Model this using 'Super Mario Bros' Level 1-1: demonstrate how the Goomba is introduced only after the player has moved right and encountered a question block, creating a safe 'tutorial' space. Emphasise that effective design avoids the 'frustration threshold' by telegraphing threats.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze notes to identify the stages of game progression. Reflect on how these stages apply to their own game concepts.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the guided notes using the provided word bank to identify how level design manages the challenge curve.
activities.questioning:
question: How do developers introduce mechanics safely in the 'Introduction' phase?
expected: By providing low-stakes areas where players can practice movement and basic interactions without immediate threat of death or reset.
question: Why is the 'frustration threshold' critical to monitor in the 'Escalation' phase?
expected: If difficulty increases too rapidly without giving the player time to achieve mastery, they become frustrated and are likely to disengage or quit.
activities.scaffolding: The Challenge Curve involves three main phases: 1. Introduction (Learning the mechanic safely). 2. Mastery (Applying the mechanic to overcome obstacles). 3. Escalation (Increasing difficulty through complexity or time limits to maintain the Flow state).
activities.eLearning: None.
activities.transition: Transition to generative task.

workbookSpec.title: The Challenge Curve and Player Flow
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the following definitions regarding game progression.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. introduction, 2. mastery, 3. escalation, 4. frustration threshold
workbookSpec.text: The game experience starts with the {{1}} phase, where the player is taught mechanics in a low-stakes environment. Once the player feels comfortable, they move to {{2}}, where they demonstrate competence through consistent success. To keep the game engaging, designers implement {{3}} by adding new obstacles or tighter timing requirements. If this slope is too steep, the player crosses the {{4}} and stops having fun.

activities.workbookMaterials: Guided notes on player experience and difficulty curves.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. introduction; 2. mastery; 3. escalation; 4. frustration threshold.

activities.title: Designing a Difficulty Slope
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that an effective difficulty curve (the 'Flow Channel') is not a straight diagonal line. Model a 'Sawtooth' curve on the board: showing how a spike in difficulty (introducing a mechanic) is followed by a slight decline or plateau as the player gains mastery. Use the example of a platformer: Level 1 introduces jumping, Level 2 introduces moving platforms, Level 3 tests mastery of both. Emphasize that dips are necessary for player recovery.
activities.studentsDo: Apply the 'Sawtooth' model to plot a 3-stage progression for their game concept. Identify the 'Introduction Point' (where stress increases) and 'Peak Mastery' (where the difficulty levels off) for each of the three levels.
activities.visibleInstructions: Sketch your 3-stage difficulty curve on the graph. Clearly label the points where you introduce a new game mechanic versus where the player achieves mastery of that mechanic. Ensure your curve trends upward over time.
activities.questioning:
question: What happens to player engagement if the difficulty curve drops suddenly to zero for a prolonged period?
expected: The player experiences boredom or 'disengagement' because the challenge no longer matches their skill level.
question: Other than increasing enemy numbers, how can you elevate challenge at the peak of a level?
expected: Increase movement speed, implement tighter time constraints, or reduce the player's resource pool (e.g., health or ammo).
activities.scaffolding: Difficulty Curve Fundamentals: 1. Introduction: New mechanic presented. 2. Acquisition: Player learns mechanic. 3. Mastery: Mechanic is used fluently. 4. Flow Channel: The ideal path where challenge matches skill.
activities.eLearning: YouTube Search: 'video game difficulty curve design theory'

workbookSpec.title: Difficulty Curve Mapping
workbookSpec.prompt: Graph your game's difficulty across three stages. Plot the 'Difficulty' (Y-axis) against 'Time/Levels' (X-axis). Draw your line reflecting the Sawtooth pattern.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: A stepped upward line where each level (1, 2, 3) starts with a spike at the mechanic introduction and a plateau/dip as mastery occurs.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: The student graph should show a general upward trajectory (progression). Specifically: Level 1 peak occurs early; Level 2 starts higher than Level 1; Level 3 is the highest peak. The 'Introduction Point' must precede the 'Peak Mastery' in every level segment. A flat line indicates poor pacing (too easy); a vertical line indicates poor pacing (unfair difficulty).

lessons.title: Visual Feedback & 'Game Juice'
lessons.learningGoal: Analyse the role of 'juice' (particle effects, screen shake, feedback) in providing clarity to player actions.

orientate.smartStart: Watch a 2-minute 'juice it or lose it' compilation (search: 'juice it or lose it game design'). Students note down 3 types of feedback observed.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can identify visual feedback techniques that improve player engagement

activities.title: Deconstructing Juice
activities.teacherDoes: Display a high-energy platforming clip (e.g., Celeste or similar) on the projector. Model the deconstruction process: 'Note the dust particles appearing at the feet upon landing (visual feedback), the slight screen zoom (camera juice), and the colour flash on the enemy (impact feedback). These features tell the player their action was successful and impactful.' Explain that 'Juice' bridges the gap between digital input and physical player satisfaction.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modelled analysis of the platforming clip. Apply the framework to annotate the provided screenshot, identifying four key instances where visual or auditory 'juice' provides clarity to player actions.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the numbered legend to annotate the game screenshot. Identify four specific instances of 'Game Juice'. Provide a brief justification for each: why is this effect used here?
activities.questioning:
question: Why does camera shake make an impact feel significantly stronger?
Expected: It simulates physical weight and energy transfer by disrupting the player's view, creating a visceral sense of impact.
question: What happens to player engagement if a combat action has zero feedback?
Expected: The action feels unresponsive, floaty, or 'dead,' leading to user confusion regarding hit detection and reduced satisfaction.
activities.scaffolding:
Common Game Juice Components: 
1. Particle Bursts (dust, sparks, smoke).
2. Screen Shake (camera displacement on impact).
3. Hit-stop / Freeze-frame (pausing animation for 1-2 frames to emphasize collision).
4. Colour Flashes (tinting objects on damage).
5. Squash and Stretch (exaggerated deformation for momentum).
activities.eLearning: YouTube Search: 'call to action website convert visitors' (concept alignment: CTA buttons use hover effects as 'juice' for clarity).
activities.transition: Transition to partner practice by swapping screenshots and comparing identified feedback elements.

workbookSpec.title: Visual Feedback Analysis
workbookSpec.prompt: Identify 4 areas of 'juice' on the provided game screenshot. Use the legend to describe the effect.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Sparks (Particle Effect): Indicates collision point. 2. Red Flash (Colour change): Indicates enemy damage. 3. Motion Blur (Visual feedback): Indicates high speed movement. 4. Camera Zoom (Screen feedback): Emphasizes critical hit.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Student must correctly identify 4 distinct feedback types. Exemplar: 1 (Particles) - Indicates impact location. 2 (Shake) - Provides weight to the explosion. 3 (Flash) - Confirms interaction status. 4 (Squash) - Demonstrates object momentum.

activities.title: Comparative Feedback Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the concept of 'digital juice' as the UX equivalent of game feedback. Model an inspection of the Keppel Bay Marina website, demonstrating how to hover over call-to-action buttons to observe state changes (e.g., colour shifts or shadow scaling). Explicitly define feedback as the 'response' to a user action, noting that without it, the user experience feels disconnected or 'dead'.
activities.studentsDo: Navigate to the designated websites. Observe interactivity by interacting with menus and call-to-action buttons. Document observations by checking off the presence of specific feedback mechanisms on their provided workbook.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Open the Keppel Bay Marina and Capricorn Coast Visitor Information websites. 2. Interact with the menus and buttons. 3. Use the checklist to audit the visual feedback provided during these interactions.
activities.questioning:
question: How does digital UI feedback correspond to 'juice' in game design?
expected: Both serve as confirmation that the system has processed a user command, reducing ambiguity and increasing user satisfaction.
question: If a button provides no visual state change, what is the consequence for the user?
expected: The user experiences 'click-uncertainty', where they are unsure if the input was registered, potentially leading to repetitive clicking and frustration.
activities.scaffolding: Definition of Feedback States: Hover (State when cursor is over an element), Active (State when the element is being clicked), and Visually Distinct (The element appears different from the static background).
activities.eLearning: Students require a web browser to access: https://www.keppelbaymarina.com.au/ and https://www.capricorncoast.com.au/.
activities.transition: Transition to independent application by collating audit findings for the upcoming design phase.

workbookSpec.title: UX Feedback Audit Checklist
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate the presence of interaction feedback on the assigned websites.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Expected: Students should note that 'Call to Action' buttons often change colour or scale upon hover (e.g., Keppel Bay Marina menu items).
items: Hover effect (colour change or underline) on navigation links
Cursor change (pointer/hand) over interactive elements
Visual shift/animation during button click (Active state)
Clear distinction between clickable buttons and static text
Immediate system responsiveness after clicking a link

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Students evaluate sites against the checklist. A 'Yes' for Hover effects should be common on professional sites like Keppel Bay Marina. If an element lacks these, students should note 'Absent'. Successful design relies on these specific cues to reduce 'dead' interaction feel.

activities.title: Feedback Loop Design
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that 'juice' is not just aesthetic decoration; it is functional communication. Demonstrate by showing a character jump without feedback, then a character jump with a particle dust puff. Model the thinking: 'For our platformer, I will add a screen shake effect when the player collides with an enemy. This provides immediate, non-textual confirmation that the collision was registered, increasing the visceral feel of the game.' Direct students to use their workbook to plan their feedback loops.
activities.studentsDo: Identify and justify three specific feedback mechanics to be implemented in their group GDevelop project. Articulate the purpose of each effect in improving player agency and clarity.
activities.visibleInstructions: Brainstorm and document three distinct 'juice' elements (visual or auditory feedback) for your group project. For each, describe the action that triggers it and the intended player experience outcome.
activities.questioning: What is the simplest feedback effect to implement in GDevelop that confirms player input? Expected: Particle effects or sound triggers for actions like jumping or attacking. How does this visual feedback prevent player frustration? Expected: It provides immediate confirmation that an input was successful, preventing the player from feeling like the game is unresponsive or broken.
activities.scaffolding: Feedback examples: 1. Visual: Particle emitters (dust clouds on jump/land). 2. Visual: Screen shake or colour flash on damage taken. 3. Auditory: Distinct 'thud' or 'ping' sounds upon item collection. Definition: Feedback Loop - The system of user input followed by a perceptible response from the game, confirming the player's agency.
activities.eLearning: None.
activities.transition: Conclude the session by identifying the highest-priority feedback effect from your list for immediate implementation in the next practical block.

Reason: Emphasises impact and danger. 3. Effect: UI animation pulse. Trigger: Picking up coins. Reason: Provides immediate reward feedback.

activities.title: Game Analysis Framework
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the 'UX Analysis Framework', critical for the upcoming assessment. Model a rapid critique of a known game interaction (e.g., character movement), focusing on the trinity of UX: Clarity (does the player know what to do?), Challenge (is the flow state maintained?), and Feedback (does the game respond viscerally?). Demonstrate how to transcribe observation into reportable data, ensuring students understand that subjective feelings must be backed by design principles.
activities.studentsDo: Engage in the comparative analysis by identifying specific UX elements in the framework table. Students classify observed game interactions against the provided technical criteria, preparing their research data for the UX critique report.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the framework table to record your observations from the chosen case study. Ensure each column contains evidence-based notes on the game's UX effectiveness.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is it essential to deconstruct existing game mechanics before beginning your own development?
expected: To identify successful implementation strategies and common pitfalls, ensuring our design choices are grounded in proven UX principles.
question: How does the 'Feedback/Juice' category influence player retention?
expected: High-quality feedback loops (visual/auditory) make the game feel responsive and rewarding, which keeps the player engaged and prevents frustration.
activities.scaffolding:
The Framework Matrix: 
1. Control/Clarity: How clearly the game communicates goals and mechanics.
2. Flow & Challenge: The pacing of difficulty; how the game maintains the 'flow state' without causing anxiety or boredom.
3. Feedback/Juice: The immediate sensory response (particles, screen shake, sound) to player input.
activities.eLearning: GDevelop project documentation and the provided UX Critique Report template.
activities.transition: Transition into the research phase where students apply this framework to their selected case studies.

workbookSpec.title: Game UX Critique Framework
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate your chosen case study against these fundamental UX pillars, ensuring your notes reflect specific game events.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Control/Clarity: Students should note tutorials, UI affordances, and key mapping. Flow & Challenge: Observations should cite difficulty spikes or smooth progression curves. Feedback/Juice: Students must identify specific 'juice' elements such as particle effects on collision, haptic feedback, or sound cues responding to player actions.

activities.title: UX Research Simulation
activities.teacherDoes: Facilitate a research session focused on 'Game Feel' and User Experience. Model how to deconstruct a specific game feature (e.g., how the jump mechanic provides visual feedback) using the prompt: 'What does the user see, hear, and feel when they perform this action?' Provide targeted feedback to groups struggling to identify specific UX mechanics over general gameplay features.
activities.studentsDo: Conduct research on a selected indie game. Complete the Game Critique Profile by isolating one specific UX feature, describing its implementation, and justifying why it enhances player engagement.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Select one indie game to research. 2. Identify a specific UX feature (e.g., visual feedback/juice, challenge curve, or UI clarity). 3. Complete the 'Game Critique Profile' workbook page by justifying how this feature contributes to the game's flow.
activities.questioning:
question: How does the specific UX feature you identified create a feedback loop for the player?
expected: Expected: The feature confirms player input immediately through visual/audio cues (e.g., screen shake or sound effect), which encourages the player to continue the action.
question: If you removed this UX feature, how would the player's perception of the game's difficulty change?
expected: Expected: The game would likely feel unresponsive or 'clunky', increasing frustration because the player would not receive clear signals about their progress or failure state.
activities.scaffolding: Game Critique Checklist: 1. Input (What does the player do?), 2. Feedback (How does the game react?), 3. Flow (Does this action interrupt or sustain the rhythm of gameplay?), 4. UI/UX (Is this information necessary or clutter?).
activities.eLearning: Students access Gamasutra or GameDesignDocs via browser to locate post-mortem articles regarding their chosen indie game's development.
activities.transition: Transition students from broad analysis to specific application by referencing their findings in the upcoming project planning documentation.

Design Justification: Explain why this feature is essential for user engagement and how it could be adapted for our major project

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Model Answer: Game Title: Celeste. UX Feature: Visual Feedback (Juice). Technical Implementation: When the player dashes, the screen pauses for a frame (hit-stop), the character glows, and a sound effect triggers. This confirms the dash has been executed. Design Justification: This 'juice' makes movement feel impactful and responsive rather than floaty. For our major project, we can adapt this by adding particle effects when the player collects items to reward exploration and provide immediate sensory confirmation of success.

activities.title: Synthesising Findings
activities.teacherDoes: Model the synthesis process. Example: 'I observed that the Keppel Bay Marina site uses clear contrast for its CTA buttons. For my game, I will apply high-contrast particle effects to the primary quest objective to ensure player focus.' Direct students to use the Adaptation Plan template to bridge the gap between their critique research and their individual game design project.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the 'Adaptation Plan' workbook section. Identify a specific UX feature researched in previous activities and draft a brief strategy for integrating or modifying it for their specific project.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using your research findings, complete the Adaptation Plan. Clearly link one specific game mechanic or visual feedback element you observed to your proposed project.
activities.questioning:
question: Which identified UX feature from your research is the most transferable to your current game design?
expected: Expected: Students should identify a specific element like 'feedback loops,' 'difficulty curves,' or 'visual cues' and explain its relevance.
question: How will your proposed adaptation mitigate player frustration?
expected: Expected: Students should discuss balancing challenge with clear feedback, such as 'by adding telegraphing animations to enemy attacks'.
activities.scaffolding: Sentence starters: 'We will use [Feature Name] to improve [Specific Game Mechanic] because it provides [Benefit to User Experience].' Concepts: Visual Clarity (use of colour/shape), Pacing (introductions of mechanics), Feedback (audio/visual confirmation of success).

Ensure they move beyond generic statements to specific mechanics (e.g., UI, feedback, or difficulty).

lessons.title: Defining Functional Requirements with User Stories
lessons.learningGoal: Construct valid user stories that define game features and acceptance criteria.

orientate.smartStart: On the workbook table, match the Agile terminology (MVP, Sprint, Kanban, Backlog) to their correct definitions.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can construct user stories that define game features and acceptance criteria

activities.title: Core Agile Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define key terms using the 'As a [persona], I want to [action], so that [value]' syntax. Model a concrete example: 'As a year 10 student, I want to filter the game leaderboard by house, so that I can see how St Brendan's is performing against rivals.' Clarify that Agile terminology prioritises the 'why' over the 'how'.
activities.studentsDo: Engage with the provided terminology list to complete the definition match activity in the workbook. Students must pair the correct definition from the word bank to the industry standard Agile term to establish a foundational vocabulary.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Review the scaffolding definitions provided in the workbook. 2. Match each Agile term with its accurate definition using the provided bank. 3. Ensure all four terms are correctly paired before transitioning to user story drafting.
activities.questioning:
question: Why do developers write requirements from the user's perspective rather than the system's perspective?
expected: To ensure the feature solves a specific user need and maintains focus on end-user value.
question: What is the primary danger of writing a user story without clearly defined acceptance criteria?
expected: It creates ambiguity, making it impossible to determine when development is complete or if the feature is functional.
question: In the context of the MVP, why is 'least effort' a critical component of the definition?
expected: It prevents scope creep and allows the team to validate core learning quickly without over-engineering.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: User Story: A short, simple description of a feature told from the perspective of the person who desires the new capability. Persona: A fictional character representing a user type. Acceptance Criteria: The conditions that a software product must satisfy to be accepted by a user. MVP (Minimum Viable Product): The version of a new product which allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning with the least effort.
activities.eLearning: Students access the provided terminology definitions on the class Trello board if they require support, or refer to the printed workbook scaffold.
activities.transition: Transition from theory to application: 'Now that we understand the anatomy of a story, let's look at how to build one in your team backlogs.'

activities.title: Anatomy of a User Story
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the Agile user story format: 'As a [Persona], I want [Feature], so that [Benefit]'. Model the logic by transforming a vague requirement—'make the game harder'—into a functional user story: 'As a player, I want to increase enemy spawn rates, so that I feel challenged during gameplay.' Highlight how the 'so that' clause prevents scope creep by focusing development on the specific user need.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the cloze exercise and draft three functional user stories relevant to their game project using the established Agile formula.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Complete the cloze notes to define the anatomy of a user story. 2. Apply the formula to draft three unique features for your group's current game project. 3. Ensure each story includes a specific persona, action, and benefit.
activities.questioning: What does the 'So that' part of the story clarify for developers? Expected: The underlying user value or objective, preventing unnecessary feature bloat. If a user story lacks a specific persona, how does it alter development decisions? Expected: It creates ambiguity regarding the target audience, leading to features that may not meet the needs of the primary user.
activities.scaffolding: Formula: As a [persona], I want [action], so that [value/benefit]. Example: As a player, I want a map icon, so that I can find my objective. Roles: Player, Administrator, Tester. Benefits: improve gameplay, enhance usability, save time, increase engagement.
activities.eLearning: Students review the 'call to action' principles on YouTube to understand how feature benefits drive user engagement: https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=call+to+action+website+convert+visitors
activities.transition: Now that we have the structure, we will map these user stories to our Trello Kanban board to establish our sprint backlog.

workbookSpec.text: A user story format: As a {{1}}, I want to {{2}}, so that I can {{3}}. The {{4}} defines who is interacting with the system, whereas the {{5}} explains the expected outcome or value.

User Story Framework:

lessons.title: Establishing the Kanban Workflow in Trello
lessons.learningGoal: Configure a Trello Kanban board to visualise and track project progress.

orientate.smartStart: Quick recall: Which part of a User Story explains the 'why' behind a feature? (30 seconds).

activities.title: I-Do: Kanban Board Layout
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the setup of a project board in Trello, emphasizing the logical flow of tasks. Model the creation of the four essential columns: Backlog (all potential features), To Do (sprint-specific tasks), Doing (active tasks), and Done (finalised and validated features). Explicitly demonstrate adding a mock 'User Story' card to the Backlog, detailing acceptance criteria. Example: 'As a player, I want a scoring system so I can track my progress. Criteria: Score increases on coin pickup; score displays on HUD.'
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher’s screen-share demonstration. Open Trello and authenticate to the project workspace. Map the required column structure using the provided workbook map.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Log into your team's Trello workspace. 2. Create a new board titled '[Game Name] Sprint 1'. 3. Configure the board columns: Backlog, To Do, Doing, Done. 4. Verify column sequence corresponds to the workflow hierarchy provided in your workbook.
activities.questioning: Why should we enforce 'Work In Progress' (WIP) limits within the 'Doing' column? Expected: It prevents multitasking, identifies bottlenecks early, and maintains focus on completing high-priority items. How does moving a card to 'Done' signify team success? Expected: It validates that the card's specific acceptance criteria have been met and tested, allowing the team to progress to the next task.
activities.scaffolding: Column Definitions: Backlog: The comprehensive repository of all potential game features and bug fixes. To Do: Specific tasks committed to by the team for the current sprint duration. Doing: Tasks currently under active development. Done: Features that have passed all testing and meet acceptance criteria. Hierarchy: Kanban Boards contain Columns; Columns contain Cards; Cards contain Checklist/Criteria.
activities.eLearning: Monitor individual group boards via Trello Enterprise dashboard to ensure naming conventions align with 'Sprint 1' standards.
activities.transition: Transition to collaborative group work: 'Teams, confirm your column layout matches the board map, then begin populating your Backlog from your project requirements.'

workbookSpec.title: Kanban Board Hierarchy and Flow
workbookSpec.prompt: Map the structural hierarchy of your Kanban board. Connect the logical progression of a card from inception to completion.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Home (Board) -> Backlog (Ideas) -> To Do (Sprint Commitment) -> Doing (Active Work) -> Done (Verified Features)

activities.teacherAnswerKey: The board structure must follow a linear workflow: Backlog -> To Do -> Doing -> Done. Each column serves a specific purpose in the Agile lifecycle: Backlog stores the 'User Stories' for future sprints; To Do captures the current sprint's commitment; Doing limits 'Work In Progress' to focus efforts; Done signifies verified completion of requirements.

activities.title: We-Do: Configuring the Board
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the standard board configuration by creating a dummy board on the projector. Explicitly model adding a member via email address and labelling a card for urgency. Use the following script: 'Your Kanban board acts as the single source of truth for your development sprint. We will standardise the workflow so every team member understands exactly what is required. Please follow the checklist provided to ensure consistency across all group projects.'
activities.studentsDo: Students access their group Trello board and systematically configure the workspace. Each member verifies that their account is correctly linked to the board and that the initial column structure matches the class template. Expected: It allows for clear communication and ensures all team members understand the urgency of tasks regardless of which board they are viewing.
activities.scaffolding: Kanban Configuration Standards: 1. Columns: Backlog, To Do, Doing, Done. 2. Member Access: All team members active. 3. Label Syntax: High (Red), Medium (Yellow), Low (Green). 4. Card Requirements: User stories must have a clear acceptance criteria.

expected: The description field, specifically the Acceptance Criteria, as it contains the technical boundaries and requirements for the feature.

activities.title: I-Do: Sprint Lifecycle

activities.questioning:
question: Why is role specialisation critical during the first sprint of development?
expected: It reduces task overlap, prevents bottlenecks, and establishes clear accountability for technical dependencies.
question: If a sprint goal is unmet, what is the professional approach?
expected: Conduct a sprint retrospective to identify blockers, reassess scope, and re-prioritise incomplete tasks in the subsequent backlog.

Role Definitions:

activities.questioning:
question: Why is 'Player Movement' ranked higher than 'Sound Effects' in your implementation plan?
expected: Core mechanics are prerequisites for testing; sound effects are polish that depend on the mechanic being finalised.
question: What happens to the sprint if you assign a task to a member without confirming their current capacity?
expected: Bottlenecks occur; the task remains incomplete, potentially blocking downstream dependencies.
activities.scaffolding:
Dependency Hierarchy Rule: 
1. Foundation (Collision, Movement) – required for any interaction.
2. Logic/UI (Menus, Score counters) – required for gameplay state.
3. Asset/Polish (Sprites, Sound) – required for visual/auditory completion.

Sound Effects/Feedback (Final polish, requires functional movement to trigger audio cues).
