lessons.title: Anatomy of the Game Design Document (GDD)
lessons.learningGoal: Evaluate the purpose and essential sections of a Game Design Document (GDD) for project communication.

orientate.smartStart: On a sticky note, list three reasons why a team might fail if they do not have a written plan.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can identify the essential components of a GDD and explain why they are critical for team alignment

activities.title: Defining GDD Components
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly define the GDD as the primary project communication tool. Model by contrasting a 'Technical Specification' (logic, variables, input handling) against 'Narrative Design' (world-building, lore, character motivation). Provide examples: 'Technical Spec' defines collision physics variables; 'Narrative Design' defines the protagonist's tragic backstory.
activities.studentsDo: Students will complete the matching exercise to solidify their understanding of standard GDD components. They will map technical and creative terminology to their functional definitions found in the bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match the GDD terminology in Column 1 to the correct definition by selecting from the provided definition bank. Write the appropriate definition in the blank Match column.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must a technical specification be managed separately from the creative narrative?
expected: Technical specifications provide actionable data for developers to code mechanics, while creative narratives focus on the player experience and aesthetic tone. Blurring these causes scope confusion.
question: What is the consequence of failing to document a 'Milestone' within the GDD?
expected: Without defined milestones, project teams lack measurable objectives, leading to 'scope creep' and difficulty in tracking development progress against the final deadline.
activities.scaffolding: GDD: A living master document detailing all game aspects, mechanics, and design goals. Technical Specification: Detailed documentation of mechanics, code logic, and input handling. Art Style Guide: A reference collection for images, colour palettes, and animation rules. Milestone: A key project checkpoint used to assess progress toward completion.
activities.eLearning: Monitor student access to the shared GDD template folder; ensure read/write permissions are configured for team collaboration.
activities.transition: Transition students from the vocabulary identification task to the GDD template implementation by initiating the project planning phase.

workbookSpec.title: GDD Component Match
bank: A defined point in time to measure progress against goals.
Documentation detailing mechanics, code logic, and input handling.
A collection of reference images, color palettes, and animation rules.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Technical Specification: Documentation detailing mechanics, code logic, and input handling. Art Style Guide: A collection of reference images, color palettes, and animation rules. Milestone: A defined point in time to measure progress against goals.

activities.title: Structuring the GDD
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model the GDD structure by presenting a 'Design Fiction' document. Demonstrate the correlation between the documentation and production workflow, highlighting: 1. How the Concept section defines the vision. 2. How the Mechanics section dictates the GDevelop logic requirements. 3. How the Assets list acts as an inventory for the art pipeline. 4. How the Timeline (Milestones) creates accountability within the team (e.g., Kanban cards).
activities.studentsDo: Engage with the GDD template via the digital workspace, actively listening to the structural breakdown and completing the guided notes to ensure conceptual alignment.
activities.visibleInstructions: Fill in the missing terms in the notes below to identify the purpose of each GDD section. Use the provided word bank to ensure accurate terminology.
activities.questioning:
question: How does the GDD link to a Kanban board like Trello?
expected: The GDD contains the high-level specifications and requirements; Trello tasks are the specific actionable items derived from those GDD sections.
question: Why is a strictly maintained Asset List vital for game development?
expected: It prevents development bottlenecks or 'crunch' by ensuring all required media, sprites, and sound effects are accounted for before implementation begins.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions: 
- Concept: The high-level vision, genre, and unique selling point of the game.
- Mechanics: The rules, controls, and gameplay loops (e.g., character movement, health systems).
- Assets: A directory of all media (art, sound, UI elements) required for the project.
- Milestones: The specific dates and progress markers used to track development stages.
activities.eLearning: Open the St Brendan's College shared GDD Template in your project folder.
activities.transition: Transition to collaborative synthesis by opening the Kanban board and mapping the GDD sections to specific task columns.

workbookSpec.title: GDD Structural Components
workbookSpec.prompt: Complete the statements below regarding GDD documentation.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Concept, 2. Mechanics, 3. Assets, 4. Milestones
workbookSpec.text: The project {{1}} serves as the overarching vision, defining the game's genre and core appeal to the player. Detailed {{2}} are necessary to describe the specific rules, inputs, and feedback loops within GDevelop. A comprehensive inventory of {{3}} ensures that all necessary visual and audio elements are organised before the build phase commences. Finally, project {{4}} are essential for dividing the development process into manageable periods, allowing the team to measure progress against deadlines.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Concept; 2. Mechanics; 3. Assets; 4. Milestones

activities.title: One-Pager Generation
activities.teacherDoes: Model the 'elevator pitch' technique for a GDD. Explain that the One-Pager serves as the project's 'source of truth' for stakeholders. Provide a worked example on the whiteboard for a simple platformer: 'The game is a 2D side-scrolling platformer that challenges players to navigate hazardous environments using a momentum-based grapple mechanic, targeting teen gamers who enjoy skill-based challenges.'
activities.studentsDo: Draft a concise project one-pager in the workbook. Students must articulate the core loop (what the player does), the primary challenge (the conflict), and the unique hook (the differentiator).
activities.visibleInstructions: Draft a one-page project summary. Ensure the Core Gameplay Loop clearly defines the player's primary action. Define your target audience beyond general demographics.
activities.questioning:
question: Does your target audience description focus on player behaviour and interests rather than just age?
Expected: The audience should be linked to specific gaming motivations (e.g., competitive players, puzzle solvers).
question: Is the 'Unique Selling Point' distinct from the genre requirements?
Expected: The USP should be an innovation or twist, not a standard feature (e.g., not just 'it has guns', but 'you control gravity to dodge projectiles').
activities.scaffolding:
Sentence starters for the sections:
1. Game Concept: 'The game is a [Genre] that challenges players to [Core Action] by using [Main Mechanic].'
2. Target Audience: 'The primary audience is [Group] who value [Specific Gaming Experience].'
3. USP: 'What sets this apart from existing titles is [Differentiator].'

lessons.learningGoal: Apply Agile project management principles to schedule development milestones and map tasks to a Kanban workflow.

orientate.smartStart: What is the difference between a task (doing) and a milestone (done)?
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can translate GDD requirements into actionable milestones on a Trello board

activities.title: Modeling the Workflow
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the transition from the Game Design Document (GDD) to a task-based Kanban system. Using a 'Player Movement' mechanic as an example, break the feature down into actionable cards: 1. Asset Creation (Sprites), 2. Scripting (Physics), 3. Audio Integration (Sound FX). Emphasize that each card requires a clear 'Definition of Done' to avoid scope creep.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the decomposition process and the alignment of GDD features to project management workflow. Students will evaluate why specific tasks are placed in distinct columns.
activities.visibleInstructions: Follow the demonstration of converting GDD requirements into Trello/Kanban cards. Analyze how vague goals are decomposed into granular, trackable tasks.
activities.questioning: Why is 'Make the Game' an ineffective project card? Expected: It is too large and vague; it lacks specificity for task tracking and progress measurement. Where should unresolved bugs be categorized within the workflow? Expected: They should move to a 'Testing/Refinement' column for iterative fix cycles.
activities.scaffolding: Kanban Column Definitions: 1. Backlog (Ideas/Requirements), 2. To Do (Prioritized tasks), 3. In Progress (Active work), 4. Testing/Refinement (Review/Bugs), 5. Done (Completed features).

workbookSpec.title: Call to Action and Conversion Design
workbookSpec.prompt: Search the provided terms to understand how digital interfaces use clear 'Call to Action' buttons to guide user flow, mirroring how your game mechanics guide player engagement.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Effective CTAs use imperative verbs (e.g., 'Start', 'Play', 'Download') and high-contrast design to reduce cognitive load, similar to how clear Kanban tasks reduce development friction.
workbookSpec.name: topic video
workbookSpec.searchTerms: call to action website convert visitors

activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Why decompose tasks? To ensure manageability and accurate time estimation. 2. Definition of Done: The state where a task meets all quality criteria (e.g., code functions, asset rendered, sound loop implemented). 3. Workflow Logic: Tasks flow from left to right; blockers or bugs are never left in 'In Progress', but are moved to 'Testing/Refinement'.

activities.title: Developing the Sprint Flow
activities.teacherDoes: Model the logic of an Agile sprint cycle, specifically focusing on the decision-making step where a feature is either accepted or requires iteration. Provide an example: 'If we test the player movement mechanic and it fails to register jump input consistently, we cannot move to Done; we must loop back to Refine.' Draw this loop on the whiteboard to clarify the visual flow.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the 'Sprint Cycle' flow chart, ensuring the logic gate (the decision point) is correctly labelled to reflect iterative design.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the provided steps to map the development cycle. Label the diamond-shaped decision node correctly: Is the mechanic functional and bug-free? Use 'Yes' to progress to 'Done' and 'No' to return to 'Refine'.
activities.questioning:
Why is the loop back to 'Refine' critical in game development? Expected: To ensure that technical debt or bugs do not accumulate in the build.
How does this flow prevent 'scope creep'? Expected: By enforcing validation stages before a task is considered closed.
activities.scaffolding:
Sprint Cycle Key Terms: 
1. Task Selection: Drawing a ticket from the backlog. 
2. Develop Prototype: Implementing code or assets in GDevelop. 
3. Test Mechanic: Running the scene to check logic. 
4. Feedback/Refine: Updating the GDD or GDevelop objects based on issues. 
5. Done: Feature is production-ready.
activities.eLearning: Use the GDevelop interface 'Preview' function as the 'Test' phase reference.
activities.transition: Transition to independent audit of the team GDD to ensure task milestones match the Sprint cycle.

workbookSpec.title: Agile Sprint Cycle Path
workbookSpec.prompt: Map the movement of a game development task through your sprint cycle.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Task Selection -> Develop Prototype -> Test Mechanic -> [Decision: Functional?] -> (No: Feedback/Refine) -> (Yes: Move to Done)

activities.workbookMaterials: Printable Flowchart Worksheet: Sprint Cycle Mapping
activities.teacherAnswerKey: The correct flow is: Task Selection (Start) -> Develop Prototype -> Test Mechanic -> [Decision Point] -> If 'No', go to 'Feedback/Refine' then loop back to 'Develop Prototype'. If 'Yes', proceed to 'Move to Done' (End).

activities.title: Milestone Audit
activities.teacherDoes: Circulate throughout the classroom, reviewing the milestone plans groups have drafted in their GDD. Use the following prompt to facilitate reflection: 'If this milestone were a level in a game, could the player clearly identify when they have finished it?' Model the correction of a vague milestone: 'Instead of 'Work on character assets', change this to 'Complete character sprite sheet including idle and run animations'.'
activities.studentsDo: Conduct a peer review of their own team's project milestones using the audit checklist. Each team member must agree on the validity of the milestones before ticking the boxes.
activities.visibleInstructions: Audit your project milestones against the Agile success criteria checklist below. If any criteria are not met, adjust your project schedule immediately.
activities.questioning: Is your first milestone too big? Expected: If the milestone requires more than two weeks of development time, it is likely too broad and needs to be decomposed into smaller tasks. What happens if you miss a milestone? Expected: We must re-evaluate our sprint scope, adjust resources, or extend the sprint duration without compromising the core game loop.
activities.scaffolding: SMART Milestone Criteria: 1. Specific: Clearly defined end-state (e.g., 'Player jump mechanics implemented'). 2. Measurable: Success can be tested/verified. 3. Achievable: Within current team capacity. 4. Relevant: Essential to the game's core loop. 5. Time-bound: Fixed to a specific calendar date.
activities.eLearning: Teachers will monitor Trello or Jira Kanban boards to verify that milestones identified in the audit checklist correlate directly to columns and cards in the live project management environment.
activities.transition: Transition to final reflections. Ensure all GDD documents are saved to the project repository for ongoing reference.

workbookSpec.title: Project Milestone Audit
workbookSpec.prompt: Evaluate your team's upcoming milestones using this quality assurance checklist.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: All items should be ticked for a healthy, Agile-compliant project sprint. If any items remain unticked, the project team must revisit their GDD and schedule.
items: Milestone has a verifiable 'Definition of Done'.
Milestone is scheduled within a 2-week sprint window.
Milestone maps directly to a specific Game Design Document section.
Dependencies between this milestone and others are identified.
All team members have assigned tasks within this milestone.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: The teacher should look for 100% completion of the checklist. If a student group leaves any item unticked, the teacher intervention should focus on breaking down the 'Milestone' into smaller, manageable 'Sprints' or tasks, as per Agile methodology. 'Definition of Done' should be specific (e.g., 'Collision detection is functional' vs 'Work on collision').

activities.title: Defining Requirements
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that user stories define functionality from the user perspective, aligning development with the player experience. Model: 'As a player, I want to collect energy orbs, so that my score increases.' Explicitly link this to project specifications (GDD).
activities.studentsDo: Translate their identified core game mechanics into formal user stories using the provided structure.
activities.visibleInstructions: Write 2 user stories for your core game mechanics using the format: As a... I want to... so that... Ensure your 'so that' statement reflects a specific game outcome or player motivation.
activities.questioning:
question: Does the user story define the 'why'?
expected: Yes, the 'so that' part explains the game loop benefit.
question: Can this be tested?
expected: Yes, the mechanic either works or it doesn't.
activities.scaffolding: Structure: As a [User], I want to [Action], so that [Goal/Benefit]. Example: As a player, I want to jump, so that I can avoid obstacles. A user story focuses on the 'what' and 'why', not the 'how'.

workbookSpec.title: Core Mechanic User Stories
workbookSpec.prompt: Draft two user stories based on your primary game mechanics.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. As a player, I want to collect coins, so that I earn points to progress to the next level. 2. As a player, I want to jump over enemies, so that I avoid losing health.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Example Student Response: 1. As a player, I want to equip a shield, so that I am protected from projectiles. 2. As a player, I want to save my progress at checkpoints, so that I do not lose significant game time upon failure. These stories clearly articulate the persona, the mechanic, and the design intent.

activities.title: Visualising the Core Loop
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly demonstrate how to break a core mechanic into a 4-frame storyboard. Example: A character jump. Frame 1 (Before): Player stance. Frame 2 (Input): Input event (e.g., Spacebar) and initial velocity. Frame 3 (During): Apex of jump, environment parallax. Frame 4 (After): Landing recovery and dust particle effect. activities.title: Layering Concepts
activities.teacherDoes: Model the definition and application of Z-order and layers within a game development context. Demonstrate how GDevelop's layer management system allows for visual depth control, including the ability to hide or show specific layers to control object visibility and interaction. Explain the role of tilemaps as an efficient method for level geometry construction, providing examples of their use in various game genres.

activities.questioning:
question: How does strategic use of Z-order contribute to player immersion and visual clarity in a game level?
expected: It ensures objects appear in a logical depth order, preventing visual confusion and enhancing the perception of three-dimensional space, which aids immersion.
question: Beyond visual organisation, what is a functional benefit of separating game elements into distinct layers?
expected: Layers can be used to control object interactions, apply unique effects or parallax scrolling to different visual planes, and optimize rendering performance by enabling or disabling specific rendering passes.
question: In what scenarios would dynamically hiding or showing a layer be a critical gameplay mechanic?
expected: For revealing hidden paths, creating temporary user interface elements like pause menus or inventory screens, or triggering environmental changes and narrative progression based on player actions or events.
activities.scaffolding:
Reference definitions:
*   **Layer:** A designated rendering plane within a game engine, grouping objects that share similar visual depth or functional properties. Layers control what objects are drawn together and how they interact visually, enabling complex scene composition.
*   **Z-order:** A numerical value assigned to objects or layers that dictates their drawing order along the depth (Z) axis. Objects with higher Z-order values are typically drawn in front of those with lower values, crucial for visual hierarchy.
*   **Tilemap:** A system used to construct game levels efficiently by arranging a grid of small, reusable graphic assets (tiles). Tilemaps are often placed on specific layers to form the primary level geometry, backgrounds, or collision maps.

3 things I learned about visual layers in game design:
1. Layers help separate different elements of a game level, like backgrounds, playable platforms, and foreground effects, to create an illusion of depth.

activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the fundamental principles of constructing effective survey questions for user feedback. Focus on ensuring clarity and specificity to prevent misinterpretation, and rigorously avoiding leading questions to maintain impartiality. Model the strategic application of both open-ended questions, designed to elicit detailed qualitative insights, and closed questions, structured for quantifiable data collection. Demonstrate the transformation of a vague or biased question, such as 'Was the game fun?', into an effective open-ended query like 'What aspects of the game design contributed most to your sense of achievement or frustration?' and a precise closed question such as 'On a scale of 1 to 5, how intuitive did you find the game's control scheme? How does the specificity of a question impact the usefulness of the feedback collected? Expected: Highly specific questions yield precise, actionable feedback that can directly inform design iterations, whereas vague questions result in general, less useful data that is difficult to act upon.

activities.title: Modelling Neutral Observation
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the critical importance of neutral observation in playtesting – observing without interference or leading the player. Project the 'Neutral Playtest Observation Log' template and model filling it out while narrating the thought process aloud. Demonstrate what to look for (e.g., player hesitation, specific actions, expressed emotions, points of confusion or delight) and how to log it objectively. Emphasise describing 'what happened' rather than 'why it happened' (e.g., 'Player repeatedly pressed jump' vs. 'Player was bad at jumping'). Use a short, simple gameplay video (pre-selected or live demonstration) as the observation subject for the model.

activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher modelling neutral playtest observation and listen to the explanation of key principles. Focus on how observations are made without interference or interpretation, using the provided log template.
activities.questioning:
Why is it crucial for an observer to remain neutral and avoid giving hints during a playtest? Expected: To gather genuine, unfiltered feedback and avoid influencing the player's natural experience or problem-solving process.
What kind of non-verbal cues or actions might indicate a player is experiencing frustration during a game? Expected: Sighs, tensing up, repeated attempts at the same action, looking away from the screen, or aggressive button presses. How might these be objectively recorded? Expected: 'Player clenched jaw', 'Repeated button press 5 times in 10 seconds', 'Stared at ceiling for 3 seconds'.
activities.scaffolding:
Provide clear examples contrasting neutral observation with biased interpretation:
Neutral: 'Player pressed the 'Jump' button three times rapidly before crossing the gap.'
Biased: 'Player struggled with the jump mechanics because they didn't understand the controls.'
Neutral: 'Player's facial expression changed from neutral to a frown when the character encountered the enemy.'
Biased: 'Player was annoyed by the enemy's unfair attack.'
Focus on observable actions, expressions, and verbalisations only.
activities.transition: Now that you've seen how neutral observation is performed, let's practice this skill together as a class using a more detailed log and a new gameplay segment.

Demonstrate identifying patterns and recurring issues by tallying similar feedback points. For instance, project a simplified sample of collected data:
*   **Player 1:** Qualitative: 'Map confusing, got lost near the oval.' Quantitative: Navigation Clarity = 2/5.
*   **Player 2:** Qualitative: 'Controls clunky, objective unclear.' Quantitative: Control Responsiveness = 2/5, Navigation Clarity = 3/5.
*   **Player 3:** Qualitative: 'Struggled to see path, map icons indistinct.' Quantitative: Navigation Clarity = 2/5, Visual Clarity = 2/5.
Model synthesising these findings, explicitly stating: 'If two players mentioned 'map confusing' or 'struggled to see path', and multiple players rated 'Navigation Clarity' low, this identifies a strong pattern. How can you differentiate between a 'recurring issue' and a one-off comment from a single player? Expected: A recurring issue is mentioned by multiple players or consistently observed across different playtests/players, indicating a systemic problem rather than individual preference.

*   **Player 2:** Controls were a bit clunky, especially turning corners. Also, the objective wasn't clear.

Quantitatively, 'Navigation Clarity' received consistently low ratings (2, 3, 2). This indicates a systemic problem with players understanding the game's map and finding their way.
2.  **Visual Clarity:** This appears to be a medium-priority issue, linked to navigation.
    *   **Evidence:** P3 mentioned 'struggled to see path in some areas' and 'map icons hard to distinguish'. Quantitatively, 'Visual Clarity' also had a low average rating (3, 3, 2), suggesting that visual presentation might contribute to navigation difficulties.
3.  **Control Responsiveness:** This is a lower-priority issue at this stage.
    *   **Evidence:** Only P2 explicitly mentioned 'controls were a bit clunky'. The quantitative ratings for 'Control Responsiveness' were mixed (3, 2, 4), indicating it may not be a universal issue but warrants further monitoring in subsequent playtests.

Include a clear task description, an estimated effort level (Small, Medium, or Large, defined by anticipated development time), and the intended positive impact on player experience (e.g., 'Enhance player agency and control satisfaction'). activities.questioning:

activities.scaffolding:
To assist in drafting your Kanban cards, consider the following definitions:
*   **Task Description:** A clear, concise statement of what needs to be done. (e.g., 'Implement a health bar UI element.')
*   **Estimated Effort:** An assessment of the development time and complexity required.
    *   **Small:** < 1 day effort, minimal complexity (e.g., adjusting a single variable).
    *   **Medium:** 1-3 days effort, moderate complexity (e.g., implementing a new simple feature).
    *   **Large:** > 3 days effort, significant complexity (e.g., major system overhaul).
*   **Expected Impact on UX:** A statement describing how this refinement will improve the player's experience (e.g., 'Reduces player frustration by clearly showing health status.')

activities.title: Debugging Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the key terms for today's lesson using precise QCAA curriculum language. Define 'bug' as an error in code, 'debugging' as the systematic process of finding and fixing errors, 'edge case' as an unexpected scenario occurring at operational extremes, and 'reproducible bug' as an issue that can consistently be triggered. Explain why clear definitions are crucial for effective technical communication within a development team. Model how to approach matching terms concisely by reading through the definition bank and locating operational keywords.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is it important for a development team to have a shared understanding of terms like 'edge case'?
expectedAnswer: To ensure clear communication when discussing technical issues, preventing misunderstandings and enabling efficient identification of complex logic flaws.
question: What might be the impact if a bug is not 'reproducible'?
expectedAnswer: It is significantly harder to diagnose the root cause and verify whether a fix has successfully resolved the issue, as the behavior cannot be reliably triggered.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions Bank:
A. An error or flaw in a computer program that causes it to produce an incorrect or unexpected result or to behave in unintended ways.
B. The process of identifying, analysing, and removing errors or bugs from computer hardware or software.
C. A problem or situation that occurs at an extreme (minimum or maximum) operating parameter, often leading to unexpected behaviour.
D. An error that can be consistently triggered or caused to occur again under specific conditions, making it easier to diagnose and fix.

activities.questioning:
Why do scene variables reset when changing scenes while global variables do not?

What happens if two scenes attempt to modify an external event sheet using different variable names?
Expected: The engine will throw a reference error or create orphan variables, breaking the shared game logic.

prompt: What causes an engine memory leak during continuous spawning of obstacle objects?

activities.title: Modeling Story Evaluation Tracing
activities.teacherDoes: Project a sample game scenario on the board. Model how to trace a functional game mechanic (e.g., player double-jump) back to a target user story. Demonstrate assessing the degree of completion: Fully Met, Partially Met, or Not Met. Model the exact syntax: As a platformer player, I want to execute a double-jump so that I can navigate tricky vertical platform gaps easily.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the modeled example on the projector. Fill in the guided user story mapping template in your workbook as modeled.
activities.visibleInstructions: Observe the teacher's demonstration. Complete the 'As a / I want / So that' blanks for the modeled double-jump feature in your workbook.
activities.questioning:
q: Why do we evaluate our final product against user stories instead of just checking if the code compiles?
Expected: User stories capture functional requirements and client/player experience goals, ensuring the game is actually playable and enjoyable, rather than just technically functional.
q: What constitutes a 'Partially Met' user story?
Expected: A feature that functions but lacks the complete acceptance criteria, such as a player jumping but without the planned landing animation or audio feedback.
activities.scaffolding: User story structure: As a [User Role], I want [Feature] so that [Benefit]. Always tie evaluation back to these three distinct components to maintain QCAA standard alignment.
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed. Focus completely on the front projector as the evaluation mapping is demonstrated.
activities.transition: Now that we have traced a single feature, we will collectively evaluate a complete scenario to align acceptance criteria.

activities.title: Group Audit of Acceptance Criteria
activities.teacherDoes: Lead a collaborative evaluation of a sample game construct. Prompt students to determine if the target acceptance criteria are fulfilled. Co-construct a checklist of indicators that prove a requirement is successfully met. Model how to verify the first item: 'Visual feedback triggers immediately upon user input' by demonstrating a button state change in the sample build. Emphasize that checking off items requires tangible evidence from the gameplay rather than assumption.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the feature checklist criteria table collaboratively as we review the sample game mechanics together, checking off functional components and noting specific evidence.
activities.visibleInstructions: With your partner, check off the criteria for the sample user experience features. Write brief observations for each checklist point to justify your verification.
activities.questioning:
If our playtest shows players find the UI controls confusing, did we meet our acceptance criteria for 'Intuitive UI'?
Expected: No, the user experience criteria failed, indicating the UI design requires further refinement to be fully functional.
How does our Trello Kanban 'Done' definition align with acceptance criteria?
Expected: A Trello card should only move to 'Done' once all corresponding acceptance criteria are verified and tested.
activities.scaffolding:
Look for explicit feedback cues: UI indicators, visual effects, and sound triggers that verify a checklist item is validated.
Full list of verification indicators:
- Input lag under 50ms
- Score increments matching game logic rules
- Collision boxes preventing out-of-bounds movement
- Audio mixing balanced without clipping.
activities.transition: With these criteria defined, you will now open your own group projects and trace your actual final builds against your original project plans.
